match.reason: The new point asks students to judge a conclusion against its evidence and to test a claim's assumptions, errors and counter-evidence, while the closest bank points teach drawing a conclusion from one's own results and judging trustworthiness of media claims, so neither teaches the same idea at the required depth.

draft.title: Judging conclusions and claims
card: Conclusion
A good conclusion answers the investigation question. It uses the evidence from the results, not guesses or opinions.
Assumptions
An assumption is something taken to be true without being checked. A claim is weaker if its assumptions may not be true.
Errors
Possible errors, such as a misread scale or a test that was not fair, can make results less reliable. They reduce how far a claim can be trusted.
Other evidence
Check whether other evidence goes against the claim. If it does, the claim needs to be questioned.
draft.remember: Trust a claim only when the evidence backs it and its assumptions, errors and opposing evidence have been checked.

opts: It answers the question using the results
It repeats the hypothesis without using results
It states what the student hoped would happen
It uses the most impressive sounding words
a.why: A good conclusion answers the question by using the evidence. Repeating the hypothesis is tempting, but it ignores what the results showed.
a.clue: What must a conclusion be based on?

b.q: An advert says Glow toothpaste whitens teeth best. It is based on one test where the only teeth tested were stained by tea. Which is the best reason to question the claim?
opts: It assumes results for tea stains apply to all teeth
The advert was written in a short sentence
The test used toothpaste rather than other products
The claim has a brand name in it
b.why: The claim assumes the tea-stain result holds for all teeth, and that has not been checked. The other options do not affect whether the evidence supports the claim.
b.clue: Ask what the claim takes for granted.

a.best: It answers the question using the results

b.best: It assumes results for tea stains apply to all teeth

problems.detail: The remember line says to trust a claim 'only when' every check has been done. The card is softer: it says errors 'can' reduce trust and that a claim is weaker if assumptions 'may' not be true. The rule is stated more absolutely than the card teaches.

The right option is the only one that repeats the stem's key detail (tea stains). The other options (brand name, short sentence, toothpaste used) are plainly irrelevant, so a student could pick the answer without understanding assumptions.

opts: It answers the question using the results
It restates the hypothesis without the results
It says what the student expected to happen
It describes the steps of the method used
a.why: A good conclusion answers the investigation question by using the evidence from the results. Restating the hypothesis is tempting, but it ignores what the results actually showed.
a.clue: What must a conclusion be based on?

b.q: A company tested Glow toothpaste and two other brands on teeth stained only by tea. Glow left the teeth whitest. Its advert says Glow whitens all stains best. Which is an assumption in the claim?
opts: Tea stains respond like every other kind of stain
Glow made the tea-stained teeth the whitest
Two other brands were tested on tea stains
The teeth in the test had tea stains on them
b.why: The test only used tea stains, so saying Glow works best on all stains takes for granted that other stains behave the same way. That was never checked. Glow making the tea-stained teeth whitest is not an assumption: it is the result the test measured.
b.clue: Which statement was never checked by the test?

a.best: It answers the question using the results

b.best: Tea stains respond like every other kind of stain
